approachQuestion.prompt:
Long Road
A vehicle starts at coordinate 0 with fuel startFuel. One unit of fuel covers one unit of distance. Stations sorted by position each offer a one-time amount of fuel; the tank has no capacity limit. Return the fewest refueling stops needed to reach target, or −1 if impossible. Arriving with zero fuel is allowed. Example: target=25, startFuel=10, stations=[(6,8),(12,9),(20,5)] → 2.

0 ≤ n ≤ 200000; 1 ≤ target ≤ 1000000000; 0 ≤ startFuel ≤ 1000000000. Each station has distinct integer position strictly between 0 and target and positive fuel ≤1000000000. Input is read-only and already sorted. Totals fit signed 64 bits. Return only the number of stops; unused stations may be passed. Which approach best meets this contract?
constraints: 0 ≤ n ≤ 200000; 1 ≤ target ≤ 1000000000; 0 ≤ startFuel ≤ 1000000000. Each station has distinct integer position strictly between 0 and target and positive fuel ≤1000000000. Input is read-only and already sorted. Totals fit signed 64 bits. Return only the number of stops; unused stations may be passed.

options.text: Maintain reach, the farthest coordinate covered by fuel selected so far, and a max-heap of unused fuel amounts at stations whose positions are at most reach. If reach is short of target, add all newly reachable stations; if the heap is empty return −1, otherwise remove its largest fuel, increase reach by it, and count one stop. Repeat until reach reaches target.
options.feedback: When more range is necessary, the largest unused reachable fuel gives at least as much extension as any other one-stop choice. Deferring that choice represents refueling at an already passed reachable station; no future station is selected prematurely.

options.text: Use a table best[s] of farthest reachable coordinate after s stops, initially best[0]=startFuel. Process stations in position order and update s downward, extending any reachable state by that station’s fuel. Return the least s reaching target.
options.feedback: This correctly prevents reusing a station, but maintains all stop-count states instead of choosing the best extension only when needed.

options.text: Whenever fuel is needed, choose the nearest unused reachable station rather than the one offering most fuel.
options.feedback: For target=20,startFuel=10,stations=[(2,1),(9,10)], choosing position 2 needs a second stop; selecting position 9 reaches target in one.

options.text: Choose the largest fuel amount anywhere on the road whenever reach is short, regardless of position.
options.feedback: For target=20,startFuel=3,stations=[(10,100)], the station is unreachable and the answer must be −1.

complexityQuestion.prompt: Analyze A with a binary max-heap, a forward station index, and scalar reach/stop count. Let n be station count. Already sorted input is not copied. Every selected fuel amount is removed from the heap; there is no route reconstruction or hashing. Choose the tightest time and auxiliary-space pair.
constraints: Use the tightest worst-case bound for the whole input unless amortized or expected accounting is explicitly specified. Comparing or moving a record and arithmetic on machine words take constant time.

Exclude supplied input and returned output from auxiliary space. Count working arrays, queues, tables and call stacks. Output storage is separate and is not used as workspace. Heap repairs and traversals are iterative. No hashing is used unless explicitly stated.

options.text: O(n log(n+1)) time, O(n) auxiliary space
O(n log(n+1)) time, O(1) auxiliary space

feedback.reason: Each station enters once and each selected fuel leaves once through the heap.
details: Each station is examined and inserted at most once, and each chosen amount is removed once. Heap repairs total O(n log(n+1)) in the worst case; cases needing many choices from a large candidate set attain this bound. The heap can hold n amounts simultaneously. With no stations the result follows from startFuel in constant time; the asymptotic bound describes growing n.
“O(n²) time, O(n) auxiliary space”: The heap method does not maintain every stop-count DP state.
“O(n) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: Variable-sized heap mutations require repairs and retain candidates.
“O(n log(n+1)) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: The input is not copied, but the candidate fuel heap still requires O(n) workspace.
